title: The Wild Wood
paragraphs: For a long time, Mole had wanted to get to know Badger. By every account Badger was a very important person, and though hardly anyone ever saw him, everyone around the place felt his unseen influence. But whenever Mole brought up his wish with Water Rat, he was always put off. “It’s all right,” Rat would say. “Badger will turn up one of these days—he’s always turning up—and then I’ll introduce you. The best of fellows! But you have to take him not only _as_ you find him, but _when_ you find him.”
“Couldn’t you invite him here for dinner or something?” said Mole.
“He wouldn’t come,” Rat said plainly. “Badger can’t stand Society, or invitations, or dinners, or anything of that kind.”
“Well, then, what if we go and call on _him?_” suggested Mole.

“Oh, I’m sure he wouldn’t care for that at _all_,” Rat said, looking quite alarmed. “He’s terribly shy and would be certain to take offense. I’ve never once dared to knock on his door myself, and I know him very well. Anyway, we can’t. It’s completely out of the question, because his home is right in the heart of the Wild Wood.”
“Well, so what if he does?” said Mole. “You told me yourself the Wild Wood was all right.”

“Oh, I know, I know, it is,” Rat said, sidestepping the question. “But I don’t think we’ll go there just now. Not _just_ yet. It’s a long way off, and he wouldn’t be at home at this time of year anyway. If you’ll only be patient, he’ll turn up one of these days.”

Mole had to be satisfied with that. But Badger never did come along, and every day brought its own pleasures. It wasn’t until summer was long over that Mole found his thoughts returning, again and again, to the solitary gray Badger, who lived his own life by himself in his hole in the middle of the Wild Wood. By then the cold and the frost and the muddy roads kept them mostly indoors, and the swollen river raced past their windows too fast for any kind of boating.

In winter Rat slept a great deal, going to bed early and getting up late. During his short day he sometimes scribbled poetry or did other small chores around the house; and of course there were always animals dropping in for a chat, so there was plenty of storytelling and comparing notes about the summer just past and everything that had happened in it.

What a rich chapter it had been, looking back on it all! And its illustrations so many, and so brightly colored! The pageant of the river bank had marched steadily along, unfolding in scene after scene that followed one another in stately procession. Purple loosestrife came early, shaking its lush, tangled locks along the edge of the mirror where its own face laughed back at it. Willow-herb, tender and wistful, like a pink cloud at sunset, was quick to follow. Comfrey, the purple one holding hands with the white, crept out to take its place in the line; and at last, one morning, the shy and lingering dog-rose stepped delicately onto the stage, and you knew, as if string music had announced it in stately chords that wandered into a gavotte, that June had finally come. One member of the company was still awaited: the shepherd-boy for the nymphs to woo, the knight the ladies waited for at the window, the prince who would kiss the sleeping summer back to life and love. But when meadow-sweet, charming and fragrant in his amber jerkin, moved graciously to his place in the group, then the play was ready to begin.

And what a show it had been! The drowsy animals, snug in their holes while wind and rain pounded on their doors, thought back to crisp mornings an hour before sunrise, when the white mist still hung close over the water. They thought back to the shock of the early dive, the scamper along the bank, and the glorious change that swept over earth, air and water when the sun suddenly rejoined them. Gray turned to gold and color was born again and sprang up out of the ground. They thought back to the drowsy siesta of a hot noon, deep in the green undergrowth with the sun slanting through in little golden shafts and spots. They thought back to afternoons of boating and bathing, rambles down dusty lanes and through yellow cornfields. And finally they thought back to the long, cool evening, when so many threads were drawn together, so many friendships rounded off and so many adventures planned for the next day. On those short winter days, with the animals gathered around the fire, there was plenty to talk about. Even so, Mole had a good deal of time on his hands. One afternoon Rat sat in his armchair before the blaze, now dozing, now fiddling with rhymes that refused to fit. So Mole decided to go out on his own, explore the Wild Wood, and perhaps get to know Mr. Badger.

The afternoon was cold and still, under a hard, steely sky, when he slipped out of the warm parlor into the open. The countryside around him lay bare and completely leafless, and it seemed to him that he had never seen so far, or so deeply, into the insides of things as on this winter day, when Nature was sunk in her yearly sleep and looked as though she had kicked off the blankets. Copses, dells, quarries and every hidden corner, which in leafy summer had been mysterious mines to explore, now lay open with all their secrets showing, pitifully, and seemed to beg him to overlook their shabby poverty for a while, until they could once more revel in rich costume and trick and lure him with the same old deceptions. In a way it was sad, and yet it was cheering—even exhilarating. He was glad he liked the country plain, harsh and stripped of its finery. Now he had reached the bare bones of it, and they were fine and strong and simple. He had no wish for warm clover or the play of seeding grasses; the screens of hedge and the billowing draperies of beech and elm seemed better out of the way. And with a very cheerful heart he pressed on toward the Wild Wood, which lay ahead of him, low and menacing, like a black reef in some still southern sea.

There was nothing to alarm him at first. Twigs crackled under his feet, logs tripped him, and fungus on the stumps looked like caricatures, startling him for a moment with their likeness to something familiar and far away; but that was all fun, and exciting. It led him on, and he pushed in to where the light was dimmer, and the trees crouched closer and closer, and the holes on either side made ugly mouths at him.
By now everything was hushed. Dusk crept up on him, steady and swift, closing in from ahead and from behind, and the light seemed to be draining away like floodwater.
Then the faces began.

At first it was only over his shoulder, and blurry, that he thought he glimpsed a face: a small, nasty, wedge-shaped face peering out at him from a hole. But when he spun around to look straight at it, the thing was gone.

He walked faster, telling himself in a cheerful voice not to start imagining things, or he would never hear the end of it. He passed one hole, then another, then another; and then—yes!—no!—yes! Beyond doubt a narrow little face with hard eyes had popped up from a hole for a moment, and vanished. He faltered—steeled himself for the effort and strode on. Then all at once, as though it had been like this from the start, every hole, near and far (and there were hundreds), seemed to have a face of its own, appearing and disappearing in a flash, each one fixing him with a stare of malice and hatred: all hard-eyed and wicked and sharp.
Once he got away from those holes in the banks, he told himself, the faces would stop. So he veered off the path and plunged into the parts of the wood where nobody ever walked.
Then the whistling began.

At first it was faint and shrill and a long way behind him; yet somehow it made him hurry on. Then, just as faint and shrill, it sounded far in front of him, and he slowed, longing to turn back. While he stood there undecided, it rose up on both sides at once, and seemed to be taken up and handed on along the entire length of the wood, right to its farthest limit. They were awake and watchful and ready, obviously, whoever they were! And he—he was alone and unarmed, miles from any help, and night was coming on.
Then the pattering began.

To begin with he took it for nothing more than falling leaves, the sound was so light and delicate. But as it swelled it settled into a steady beat, and he knew it could only be the pat-pat-pat of little feet, still a very long way off. Was it ahead or behind? First it seemed to be one, then the other, then both. It swelled and multiplied, and however he listened, anxiously, leaning one way and then another, it seemed to be tightening around him from every side. While he stood motionless, listening, a rabbit came tearing through the trees straight at him. He waited for it to slow down, or to veer away on some other path. Instead it nearly brushed against him as it shot past, its face set and hard, its eyes staring. “Get out of here, you fool, get out!” Mole heard it mutter, as it swung around a stump and vanished down a welcoming burrow.

The pattering swelled until it sounded like a sudden hailstorm on the dry carpet of leaves around him. The whole wood seemed to be running now, running hard, hunting, chasing, closing in on something or—somebody? Panic took hold of him and he began to run as well, without aim, with no idea where. He ran into things, tripped over things and tumbled into things, ducked under things and swerved around things. In the end he hid himself in the deep dark hollow of an old beech tree, which promised shelter, cover—perhaps even safety, though who could say? In any case he was too worn out to run another step, and all he could do was burrow into the dry leaves that had blown into the hollow and hope he was safe for the time being. And lying there, panting and shaking, listening to the whistling and pattering outside, he finally understood it, in its full horror, that dreadful thing which other small dwellers of field and hedgerow had met here and remembered as their blackest hour—that thing which Rat had tried, without success, to spare him from—the Terror of the Wild Wood!

Back at home, Rat sat warm and comfortable, dozing by his fire. The paper with his half-finished verses slid off his knee, his head tipped back, his mouth dropped open, and he drifted along the green banks of dream-rivers. Then a coal settled, the fire crackled and threw up a tongue of flame, and he jerked awake. He remembered what he had been busy with, reached down to the floor for his verses and frowned over them for a minute, then glanced around for Mole, meaning to ask whether he knew a good rhyme for this or that.
But Mole wasn’t there.
He listened for a while. The house seemed very quiet.
Then he called out “Moly!” a few times, and when nobody answered he stood up and walked out to the hall.
Mole’s cap was missing from its usual peg. His galoshes, which always lay by the umbrella stand, were gone too.

Rat went out of the house and studied the muddy ground by the door, hoping to spot Mole’s tracks. And there they were, plain as anything. The galoshes were brand new, bought just for the winter, and the studs on their soles were still fresh and sharp. He could see their prints in the mud, running along straight and full of purpose, heading directly for the Wild Wood.

Rat’s face turned very grave, and for a minute or two he stood lost in thought. Then he went back inside, buckled a belt around his middle, pushed a pair of pistols into it, snatched up a stout club that was standing in a corner of the hall, and set off for the Wild Wood at a brisk walk.

Dusk was already settling in by the time he came to the first scattering of trees, and he marched straight into the wood without a second thought, glancing anxiously left and right for some trace of his friend. Wicked little faces poked out of holes here and there, only to duck back out of sight when they saw the brave fellow with his pistols and the big ugly club in his fist. The whistling and pattering he had heard so clearly when he first stepped in faded away and stopped, and everything went very quiet. Boldly he pushed along the whole length of the wood until he reached its far edge. Then he left the paths behind altogether and began crossing the wood back and forth, working his way patiently over every bit of ground, calling out cheerfully the whole time, “Moly, Moly, Moly! Where are you? It’s me—it’s old Rat!”

After an hour or more of patient searching through the wood, he finally heard, to his great joy, a small voice calling back. Following the sound through the thickening dark, he came to the base of an old beech tree with a hollow in its trunk, and from inside the hollow a weak voice said, “Ratty! Is it really you?”
Rat crawled into the hollow and found Mole there, worn out and still shaking. “Oh, Rat!” he cried. “You can’t imagine how scared I’ve been!”

“Oh, I understand perfectly,” Rat said, in a soothing tone. “You really shouldn’t have done it, Mole. I tried my best to stop you. Those of us who live on the river bank almost never come here alone. When we must, we go at least in twos; then we’re usually fine. And besides, there are a hundred things you need to know, things we understand and you don’t yet. Passwords, I mean, and signs, and sayings that carry power, and plants you keep in your pocket, and verses you recite, and little tricks and dodges you practice; all easy enough once you know them, but a small animal has to know them, or he’ll land in trouble. Of course, if you were Badger or Otter, that would be a different matter altogether.”
“But surely brave Mr. Toad wouldn’t be afraid to come here on his own, would he?” Mole asked.
“Old Toad?” Rat said, with a hearty laugh. “Not on your life would he show his face here alone, not for a whole hat full of gold guineas, that Toad.”
Rat’s easy laughter did Mole a world of good, and so did the sight of that stick and those shiny pistols. His shivering stopped, and he began to feel braver and more like his old self.

“Well now,” Rat said after a moment, “we really have to pull ourselves together and start for home while a little light is left. We can’t possibly spend the night here, you see. It’s too cold, for one thing.”

“Dear Ratty,” said poor Mole, “I’m terribly sorry, but I’m completely done in, and that’s the honest truth. If I’m ever going to make it home, you _have_ to let me rest here a little longer and win back my strength.”
“Oh, fine,” said good-natured Rat. “Rest all you like. It’s nearly black as pitch out there anyway, and a bit of moon should turn up later on.”

So Mole snuggled deep into the dry leaves and stretched out, and before long he drifted off—though his sleep was restless and full of bad dreams. Rat, meanwhile, wrapped himself up as warmly as he could and lay there patiently keeping watch, a pistol held ready in his paw.
At last Mole woke up, much refreshed and feeling like himself. Rat said, “Right! I’ll just step outside and make sure all is quiet, and then we really must get going.”
He walked to the mouth of their hiding place and stuck his head outside. Then Mole heard him murmuring to himself, “Well, well! Here’s—a—pretty—how-do-you-do!”
“What’s up, Ratty?” asked Mole.
“_Snow_ is up,” Rat replied briefly; “or rather, _down_. It’s snowing hard.”

The Mole came over and crouched beside him. Looking out, he saw that the wood that had frightened him so much looked completely different now. The holes, hollows, pools, pitfalls and other black dangers for travelers were disappearing fast, and a shining carpet of fairy-work was spreading everywhere, so delicate it seemed a shame to tread on it with rough feet. A fine powder hung in the air and tingled against the cheek, and the black trunks of the trees stood out in a light that seemed to come from below.

“Ah, well, there’s no help for it,” said Rat after a little thought. “I suppose we have to set off and trust to luck. The trouble is, I’m not at all sure where we are. And with the snow, everything looks completely changed.”

It certainly did. The Mole would never have guessed it was the same wood. Still, they set off bravely along the way that looked most hopeful, holding on to each other and pretending, with unbeatable cheerfulness, that they recognized an old friend in every new tree that stared grimly and silently back at them. They pretended, too, that they spotted openings, gaps and paths with a familiar bend to them, in a dull stretch of white ground and black tree trunks that never changed.

An hour or two later—they had lost all track of time—they stopped, discouraged, worn out and hopelessly lost, and sat down on a fallen tree trunk to catch their breath and decide what to do. They ached with tiredness and were bruised from tumbling; they had fallen into several holes and were soaked through; the snow was getting so deep that they could barely drag their little legs through it, and the trees were thicker and more alike than ever. There seemed to be no end to this wood, and no beginning, and no variety in it, and, worst of all, no way out.

“We can’t sit here very long,” said the Rat. “We’ll have to make another push and do something. The cold is terrible, and soon the snow will be too deep for us to wade through.” He peered around and thought. “Listen,” he went on, “here’s what I’m thinking. There’s a sort of dip just ahead of us, where the ground looks all hilly and lumpy and bumpy. Let’s make our way down into that and look for some kind of shelter, a cave or a hole with a dry floor, out of the snow and the wind, and we’ll have a good rest there before we try again, since we’re both pretty well worn out. Besides, the snow may stop, or something may turn up.”

So once more they got to their feet and struggled down into the dip, where they searched about for a cave or some dry corner that would shelter them from the biting wind and the whirling snow. They were poking around one of the lumpy spots the Rat had mentioned when suddenly the Mole tripped and fell flat on his face with a squeal.
“Ow! My leg!” he yelped. “My poor, poor shin!” And he sat up in the snow and clutched the injured leg against him with both front paws.
“Poor old Mole!” said the Rat kindly.

“Not your lucky day, is it? Here, let me see that leg. Yes,” he continued, kneeling down to inspect it, “you’ve certainly cut your shin. Hold on while I dig out my handkerchief, and I’ll bandage it for you.”
“I must have caught my foot on some buried branch or stump,” Mole said glumly. “Oh dear! Oh dear!”

“It’s a very clean cut,” said the Rat, studying it closely again. “A branch or a stump never did that. It looks as if it was made by the sharp edge of something metal. Strange!” He thought for a while and looked over the humps and slopes around them.
“Well, never mind what done it,” said Mole, so pained he forgot his grammar. “It hurts just as much, whatever done it.”

Meanwhile Rat had finished bandaging the leg with his handkerchief, left Mole sitting there, and gone off to dig busily in the snow. He scratched, he shoveled, he poked about, all four paws hard at it, while Mole waited with growing impatience and called out every so often, “Oh, _come_ on, Rat!”
All at once Rat shouted “Hooray!” and then “Hooray-oo-ray-oo-ray-oo-ray!” and started dancing a wobbly little jig on the snow.
“What _have_ you found, Ratty?” asked the Mole, still nursing his leg.
“Come and see!” said the delighted Rat, still jigging.
The Mole limped over to the spot and took a good look.

“Well,” he said at last, in a slow voice, “I SEE it, sure enough. I’ve run into plenty of these before. Nothing out of the ordinary, if you ask me. A door-scraper! So what? Why are you jigging around over a door-scraper?”
“But can’t you see what it _means_, you—you dim-witted creature?” cried the Rat impatiently.

“Of course I understand what it means,” answered Mole. “It means that some VERY careless, absent-minded person has dropped his door-scraper in the middle of the Wild Wood, _right_ where it’s _certain_ to trip up _everyone_ who passes. Awfully inconsiderate of him, if you ask me. Once I’m home, I’m going to lodge a complaint with—with somebody or other, you just wait and see!”
“Oh, dear, oh, dear!” cried Rat, hopeless at how thick Mole was being. “Stop arguing and come help me dig!” Back he went to his shoveling, and the snow flew up around him in every direction.
After a bit more hard work his efforts paid off, and a very shabby doormat lay uncovered.
“There, what did I tell you?” exclaimed the Rat in great triumph.

“Absolutely nothing at all,” replied the Mole, with perfect truthfulness. “Now then,” he went on, “you seem to have found another bit of household rubbish, worn out and thrown away, and I suppose you’re perfectly happy. Go ahead and dance your jig around that if you must, and get it over with, and then maybe we can move on and not waste any more time on rubbish heaps. Can we EAT a doormat? Or sleep under a doormat? Or sit on a doormat and sled home over the snow on it, you maddening rodent?”
“Are—you—telling—me,” cried the excited Rat, “that this doormat doesn’t _tell_ you anything?”

“Honestly, Rat,” said Mole, rather peevishly, “I think this silliness has gone on long enough. Whoever heard of a doormat _telling_ somebody something? They don’t. They’re not the type. A doormat knows its place.”

“Now listen here, you—you blockhead,” replied the Rat, really angry, “this has to stop. Not another word, just scrape—scrape and scratch and dig and search around, especially on the sides of the lumps, if you want to sleep warm and dry tonight, because it’s our last chance!”

The Rat attacked a snowbank beside them with enthusiasm, probing everywhere with his stick and then digging furiously; and the Mole scraped busily too, more to please the Rat than for any other reason, since he thought his friend was getting light-headed.

After some ten minutes of hard work, the tip of the Rat’s stick struck something that sounded hollow. He kept working until he could get a paw through and feel around; then he called the Mole to come and help. The two animals went at it hard, until at last the result of their labor stood in full view of the astonished and, until now, doubting Mole.

In the side of what had looked like a snowbank stood a solid little door, painted dark green. An iron bell-pull hung beside it, and below that, on a small brass plate, neatly engraved in square capital letters, they could read by the light of the moon
MR. BADGER.

Mole was so astonished and delighted that he toppled backward into the snow. “Rat!” he cried, quite ashamed of himself. “You’re a marvel! A genuine marvel, that’s what you are. Now I see the whole thing! Right from the moment I fell and cut my shin, you reasoned it out one step at a time inside that wise head of yours. You looked at the cut, and straight away your magnificent mind told you, ‘Door-scraper!’ Then you went and tracked down the very door-scraper that did the damage! And did you stop there? No. Plenty of people would have been content, but not you. Your brain kept right on going. ‘If I can only turn up a doormat,’ you said to yourself, ‘my theory will be proven!’ And naturally you found your doormat. You’re so clever I believe you could find anything you pleased. ‘Now,’ you say, ‘that door is as good as standing in front of me. All that’s left is to find it!’ I’ve read about this sort of thing in books, but I never saw it happen in real life. You belong somewhere you’ll be properly admired. You’re wasted here among ordinary folks like us. If I only had your brains, Ratty——”

“Since you haven’t,” snapped the Rat, rather unkindly, “I suppose you plan to sit in the snow all night and _talk?_ Up you get, this minute! Hang on to that bell-pull over there and ring it hard, as hard as you can, while I pound on the door!”

Rat set about pounding on the door with his stick, while Mole leaped up and caught hold of the bell-pull. He hung there swinging with both feet dangling in the air, and from somewhere far inside they could just make out the faint answer of a deep-voiced bell.
